title: Start here: Glow Card (your first lithophane)
summary: Choose a safe photo, predict how thickness changes light, and build a picture that glows.
objective: Students choose a photo they have the right to use, predict where a lithophane will be thick or thin, and compare the preview with their prediction.
teacher_notes: START HERE lesson. The printer is operated by the teacher or a trained adult; students design and preview only. Printing takes time (test one on your own printer first and write the real number on the board; do not rely on a generic estimate). Offer a school-safe image pack (pets, landscapes, objects, student drawings, public-domain images) so no one has to use a personal photo. Use LED tea-lights only.

steps.title: Pick a photo you are allowed to use
steps.body: Choose a photo you took yourself, a drawing you made, or one from the class image pack. Do not use a photo of another person unless they said yes (and for school use, ask your teacher first). Good picks: a pet, a plant, a toy, a landscape, your own drawing. Do not use photos that show your home address, school name or a license plate.

steps.title: Predict before you build
steps.body: Look at your photo. Which parts are dark? Which are bright? Sketch or say: where will the plastic be thick, and where thin? Remember: thick blocks light (looks dark), thin lets light through (looks bright).

steps.title: Build it
steps.body: In the Studio choose Lithophane, keep Beginner mode, pick Standard, and press Build. Check that the preview shows your picture.

steps.title: Compare with your prediction
steps.body: Was your prediction right? Try Thin and Thick and compare. Write one sentence: what changed when the plastic got thicker?

steps.title: Ask your teacher to print it
steps.body: Tell your teacher your model is ready. Your teacher runs the printer. Stay away from hot parts and keep your hands off the printer while it works.

steps.title: Light it safely
steps.body: Put a small LED tea-light behind the finished panel. Never use a hot bulb: plastic can bend or melt.

quiz.q: Which choice is a good photo for this project?
options: A classmate's face, taken without asking
Your own drawing or a pet photo you took
A picture showing your home address on a sign

title: Height Detectives: feel a picture
summary: Learn that bright can mean tall by drawing a bold shape and touching the printed relief.
objective: Students describe a relief as 'taller in some places, flatter in others' and match a drawing to the raised shape they feel.
teacher_notes: Teacher-led, one device at the front. Students draw with thick dark marker on white paper; the teacher photographs/scans a few drawings (no faces, no names on the paper). Pre-print one tactile relief. Offers a tactile route in for students who learn by touch, including students with low vision; check with your vision specialist.

steps.title: Touch first
steps.body: Pass around a printed relief. Close your eyes if you like. Where does it feel tall? Where does it feel flat?

steps.title: Draw a bold shape
steps.body: Draw one big, simple shape (a star, a fish, a house) with a thick marker. Keep it high-contrast.

steps.title: Teacher builds it
steps.body: Your teacher puts the drawing into the Studio as Relief. Watch the picture turn into a 3D shape on the screen.

steps.title: Match it
steps.body: Which drawing became which shape? Point to the tall part and the flat part.

quiz.q: In a relief made from a picture, what do bright parts usually become?
options: The same height as dark parts

title: Name Tag Engineers: measure, base, initials
summary: Measure in millimetres, add a base, and emboss initials (not full names) on a small tag.
objective: Students measure a model in millimetres, explain why a flat base helps a print stand or stick, and test one change at a time.
teacher_notes: Uses the Edit workspace (scale, base, text, measure). Use INITIALS or a team symbol, not full names, if tags will be displayed. A ruler per pair. Note: the Spark Lab 'Try it' button currently opens the Studio only; open Edit from the top navigation.

steps.title: Measure a real thing
steps.body: Use a ruler to measure your pencil case in centimetres, then in millimetres. Which number is bigger? Why?

steps.title: Open the sample
steps.body: In Edit choose 'Open sample'. Use the Measure tool to find how wide the model is in mm.

steps.title: Scale it
steps.body: Scale the model so it is about 40 mm wide. Check with Measure.

steps.title: Add a base
steps.body: Press 'Add base'. Why do you think a flat base helps?

steps.title: Add initials
steps.body: Add text with your initials. Change only ONE thing, then look at the result.

steps.title: Share a result
steps.body: Tell a partner one thing you changed and what happened.

quiz.q: A tag is 40 mm wide. How many centimetres is that?

title: Layer Cake Posters: pop-art colours as height
summary: Reduce a picture to a few colour layers, stack them, and critique designs kindly.
objective: Students explain how a picture can be simplified into N flat layers, predict how layer count and step height change total height, and give specific, kind feedback using a protocol.
teacher_notes: Use class-pack or student-created images. Teach the critique protocol 'I notice... I wonder... What if...' before students look at each other's work. Math tie-in: total height = layers x step. Feedback stays inside the class; do not publish student work.

steps.title: Choose a bold image
steps.body: Pick an image with clear shapes from the class pack or your own artwork.

steps.title: Predict the layers
steps.body: If you use 4 colours, how many layers will stack? If each layer is 1 mm, how tall will the poster be?

steps.title: Build it
steps.body: In the Studio choose Pop-art. Try 3, 4 and 6 colours. Compare.

steps.title: Check your maths
steps.body: Open the model details. Does the height match your prediction?

steps.title: Kind critique
steps.body: With a partner use: I notice... I wonder... What if...? Give one specific, kind comment each.

steps.title: Revise
steps.body: Change one setting based on the feedback and rebuild.

quiz.q: A pop-art model has 5 layers of 1 mm each. About how tall are the layers together?

title: Fit Check: measure, tolerance, redesign
summary: Design a part that has to fit a real object, test the fit, and document one redesign.
objective: Students measure a real object, design a part with a stated tolerance, test it, and justify one design change with evidence.
teacher_notes: Engineering design cycle: define, measure, make, test, improve. Use a safe, non-hazardous target object (a pencil, a marker cap, a USB stick cover). Provide calipers if available. Teacher or trained student operator runs the printer. This lesson needs two print cycles; plan extra days for printer errors.

steps.title: Define the problem
steps.body: Pick a small object that needs a holder, cap or cover. Write the requirement in one sentence and one number (for example: 'must slide on with about 0.3 mm of space').

steps.title: Measure
steps.body: Measure the object in mm at least twice and record the numbers.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: In Edit start from the sample or a photo base, use scale, base, and a boolean cut to make the opening. Record your numbers.

steps.title: Check and repair
steps.body: Run Repair, then Measure again. Does the model match your plan?

steps.title: Print and test
steps.body: Your teacher prints it. Test the fit and write what you observe.

steps.title: Redesign
steps.body: Change ONE dimension, explain why using your measurements, and print again if time allows.

quiz.q: Why change only one dimension per test?
options: So you know which change caused the result
